blocks.content: Metamorphic rocks are formed under the action of pressure, volume and temperature (PVT) changes.

blocks.title: Key Takeaways
items: Metamorphic rocks are formed when existing sedimentary or igneous rocks undergo recrystallization and mineral reorganization due to changes in Pressure, Volume, and Temperature (PVT).
Dynamic metamorphism occurs without significant chemical change through crushing and mechanical breakdown caused by intense directed pressure.
Thermal metamorphism occurs when high temperatures alter rock composition, divided into Contact Metamorphism (magma contact) and Regional Metamorphism (tectonic pressure and heat).
Foliation or Lineation is the arrangement of mineral grains or crystals in parallel layers within metamorphic rocks.
Key rock transformations include Granite to Gneiss, Clay/Shale to Slate, Limestone to Marble, and Sandstone to Quartzite.

rows: Direct contact with hot magma or lava intrusions
Tectonic deformation associated with mountain building
Widespread regional areas across hundreds of kilometers
Combined High Pressure and High Temperature

items: Frequently tested parent-to-metamorphic conversions: Limestone -> Marble, Sandstone -> Quartzite, Clay/Shale -> Slate -> Schist, Granite -> Gneiss, Coal -> Anthracite/Graphite.
Differentiate between Foliation (parallel alignment of mineral grains) and Banding (alternating thick and thin layers of light and dark minerals).

Contact metamorphism produces non-foliated rocks (e.g., Marble, Hornfels) due to heat, while Regional metamorphism produces foliated rocks (e.g., Gneiss, Schist) due to combined regional tectonic forces.
